displayQuote: Build your opponent a golden bridge to retreat across

meta.title: Who really said "Build your opponent a golden bridge to retreat across"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Sun Tzu, in these words. There is no bridge and no gold anywhere in The Art of War. The real line is VII.36: ‘When you surround an army, leave an outlet free.’
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Build your opponent a golden bridge to retreat across'?
meta.ogDescription: The idea is Sun Tzu’s; the sentence is not. Wikiquote files it as Disputed, and no source has ever been located for the wording.

answer.label: Not Sun Tzu’s words — a modern paraphrase
answer.authorDates: No documented author · a modern English rendering
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Sun Tzu’s. The sentence is not. Search Lionel Giles’s 1910 translation end to end and the phrase ‘golden bridge’ does not occur once; the word ‘bridge’ turns up only in passages about burning them. What Sun Tzu actually wrote, at chapter VII verse 36, is ‘When you surround an army, leave an outlet free’ — and Giles’s note explains why. Wikiquote files the golden-bridge wording under Disputed, and nobody has produced an author or a first appearance for it.

source.heading: What The Art of War actually says

docMeta.dt: Source for the wording quoted here
docMeta.dd: None located — not in the text
The Art of War, ch. VII (Manœuvering), v. 36

source.excerpt: When you surround an army, leave an outlet free. […] Do not press a desperate foe too hard.
trail: We went to the text first, because that is the only thing that settles it. Giles’s 1910 translation is the standard public-domain English Art of War and it is fully searchable. Searched end to end, it contains no occurrence of ‘golden bridge’; ‘bridge’ appears only in unrelated passages, one of them about burning them the full Giles text ↗

What is there, at chapter VII verse 36, is ‘When you surround an army, leave an outlet free’, followed by ‘Do not press a desperate foe too hard’ — with Giles’s note quoting Tu Mu on making the enemy ‘believe that there is a road to safety’. That is the passage the golden-bridge line paraphrases chapter VII, verse 36 ↗

Wikiquote reaches the same conclusion independently and files the sentence under Disputed, calling it a variant of Sun Tzu’s assertion to ‘leave a way of escape’ and noting Tu Mu’s commentary. It also records that the line ‘has recently appeared on the internet attributed to Scipio Africanus, but without citation’ Wikiquote, Sun Tzu — Disputed ↗

We checked that rival credit too. Wikiquote’s own page for Scipio Africanus carries no golden-bridge entry at all — not in its quotes, not in its Disputed section. So the Scipio attribution is uncited on the page best placed to cite it Wikiquote, Scipio Africanus ↗
source.cutTag: Sun Tzŭ, The Art of War VII.36, trans. Lionel Giles (1910)
source.excerptNote: Giles prints these two sentences as one verse, separated by his own commentary — which is where the misunderstood half of the idea lives. On the first sentence Giles quotes the Tang commentator Tu Mu: the object is ‘to make him believe that there is a road to safety, and thus prevent his fighting with the courage of despair.’ Then Tu Mu, in Giles’s words, ‘adds pleasantly: After that, you may crush him.’ The genuine advice is not mercy. It is that a cornered enemy fights harder, so you should let him think he can leave.

author.name: Sun Tzu
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Sun Tzu
author.metaLine: Traditionally 544–496 BC · Chinese general and strategist · historicity uncertain
author.bio: Sun Tzu is the traditional author of The Art of War, dated by the Han historian Sima Qian to 544–496 BC and said to have served King Helü of Wu. His historical existence is uncertain: scholars from the 12th century onward have noted that the Zuo Zhuan, a detailed chronicle of exactly that period, does not mention him at all, and the earliest parts of the text probably postdate him by a century or more. He is a magnet for invented aphorisms for the usual reason — the real text is genuinely full of short, quotable strategic maxims, so a fabricated one blends in. The test never changes: which chapter, which verse?

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabrication in the ordinary sense — the strategic idea behind it really is in The Art of War. What is invented is the sentence, and once a sentence is in quotation marks it is making a claim about a text.

items.why: Searched end to end, Giles’s translation contains no ‘golden bridge’ and no gold in this connection at all. Nobody quoting the line offers a chapter or a verse, which is the standard signature of a wording invented downstream of the text search the text yourself ↗

context.heading: Why the paraphrase spread
lead: The golden-bridge image is better copy than the original. ‘Leave an outlet free’ is a flat tactical instruction; ‘build your opponent a golden bridge’ is a picture, and it flatters the reader into hearing generosity in it. That is very likely why it travelled, and it is also why it misleads.

Because Sun Tzu’s point is not generosity. Read Giles’s note and the reasoning is cold: a surrounded enemy who believes he is trapped will fight with the courage of despair, so you give him somewhere to run — and then, as Tu Mu says, you may crush him. The paraphrase keeps the tactic and loses the motive.
context.detailsSummary: How to check a Sun Tzu quotation in one move
detailsBody: Ask which chapter and verse. The Art of War is thirteen short numbered chapters — a genuine line can always be pointed at.
Search the Giles translation. It is public domain, complete, and freely searchable at Project Gutenberg.
Distrust vivid imagery. The real text is spare and administrative; ornamental metaphor in an English ‘Sun Tzu’ quotation is usually a translator’s flourish or an invention.
Beware the commentators. Much of what circulates as Sun Tzu is really Tu Mu, Ts’ao Ts’ao or Chang Yu, whose notes Giles prints alongside the text.
context.pull: The golden bridge is not mercy. It is a way of not having to fight a desperate man.
